disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by a combination of mood episodes meeting criteria for mania or mixed episodes, together with psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations that also occur outside of mood episodes. To diagnose it, there must be a period of at least two weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms, along with mood episodes present for a substantial portion of the illness. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with functional impairment that can range from moderate to severe, and it can be difficult to distinguish from bipolar I disorder with psychotic features or schizophrenia unless the temporal relationship between mood and psychosis is carefully documented. Treatment typically involves mood stabilizers and antipsychotic medications, sometimes with adjunctive psychosocial interventions to address social and occupational dysfunction.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Matthew took on a heavier caseload when his agency became short-staffed, agreeing to cover more medically complex seniors and longer shifts while still volunteering at church and the senior center. The combination of rotating hours, middle-of-the-night calls, and emotionally intense end-of-life care gradually eroded his usual structure of hunting weekends, line-dancing nights, and family barbecues that had kept him grounded. Over several months, his family and coworkers noticed that he became increasingly preoccupied with unusual ideas about his special role in protecting his clients and community, and he began to clash with supervisors as his decisions at work and church grew inconsistent with safety protocols and expectations. The functional strain—missed documentation, erratic behavior during safety briefings, and concerns raised by his pastor and wife—finally led his agency to insist on an occupational health evaluation, at which point he was referred for psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like God’s picked me out personally to fix everything in this town, and nobody understands how important my mission is.”

narrative.stressor: Around 17 months ago, Antionette decided to push hard toward her long-held goal of becoming a CNA supervisor, picking up extra shifts, enrolling in evening prep courses, and volunteering to lead art-based activities at the facility. The increased demands disrupted her usual balance of solitary painting, gardening, and quiet walks, and she began spending more nights awake planning projects and studying, insisting she could manage on very little rest. Over time, coworkers noticed her documentation became inconsistent and she grew intensely suspicious about others trying to undermine her advancement, while at home her art and crochet projects piled up half-finished as she jumped from one ambitious idea to another without follow-through. After a tense incident in which she accused a colleague of sabotaging her training and her supervisor documented a marked decline in reliability, she was urged to see her primary care provider, who referred her for psychiatric evaluation when it became clear that these thinking changes were persisting and affecting her ability to work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind just won’t slow down—ideas are racing all the time and I can’t keep my thoughts straight anymore.”

narrative.stressor: About a year and five months ago, Andres and his wife moved from their longtime house in Las Piedras into a smaller apartment closer to their adult daughter after he had a minor fall, a change that disrupted his familiar routines of tending his garden, walking the same streets, and organizing neighborhood repair projects. Although he stayed involved with church and the senior center, he felt disoriented by the new environment and increasingly withdrew from leading community events, spending more time alone in his room with the radio. Over the following months, his family noticed that he became markedly less engaged in cooking, music rehearsals, and domino games, and that he seemed oddly flat and indifferent to traditions he once cherished, even as he occasionally mentioned experiences and beliefs that did not match what others observed. When he started skipping mass and choir, stopped caring for his plants, and his daughter realized he could no longer reliably manage simple household tasks or social commitments, she arranged for a home visit from his primary doctor, who then referred him for specialized psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t feel like doing anything anymore—not cooking, not music, not even playing dominoes with my friends.”
